## Abstract

The population of extremely long-period Mira variables in the Milky Way remains poorly characterized. Their rarity and heavy circumstellar obscuration have precluded systematic studies in optical surveys, yet they are expected to trace the most massive stars evolving through the Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB). We present IRTF/SpeX spectroscopy of the longest-period ( $P\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d) Galactic Mira variables identified with the Palomar Gattini-IR survey. Twelve of thirteen targets exhibit characteristics consistent with massive O-rich AGB stars. In contrast, one peculiar source IRAS 19552+3142 exhibits i) a large-amplitude ( $\Delta J\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}2$ mag) pulsations with $P\approx 1060$ d, ii) strong C2 and CO molecular bands indicating C/O $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1$ , and iii) SiC emission at $\approx 11.3\,\mu$ m in archival mid-infrared spectra. Its spectroscopically confirmed chemistry makes it the longest period C-rich Galactic Mira variable known; together with the rarity of similar objects, this source is difficult to reconcile with standard massive AGB evolution where hot-bottom burning maintains an O-rich surface composition. Instead, its properties may be explained by super-AGB evolution where dredge-out episodes produce a C-rich surface and circumstellar material. Its high luminosity ( $M_{[4.5]}\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}-10$ mag), red color ( $[3.6]-[4.5]\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}2.0$ mag), and high mass-loss rate ( $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ ) resemble extreme AGB star progenitors of intermediate-luminosity red transients in nearby galaxies and a known chemically peculiar super-AGB star candidate in the Small Magellanic Cloud. IRAS 19552+3142 may thus provide a rare look at a Galactic super-AGB star in the thermally pulsing phase. Our results motivate improved theoretical predictions and long-baseline infrared searches for these short-lived, dust-enshrouded endpoints of stellar evolution.

## I Introduction

Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars represent the end fates of most stars in the universe [83]. While lower mass ( $\approx 1-2$ M⊙) AGB stars are routinely identified as Mira variables with periods in the range of $100-300$ d (e.g., Sanders 59), the evolution of higher mass AGB stars and their final remnants remains unclear [60]. While the general evolution of AGB stars is well understood, the late evolutionary stages and final fates of the most massive AGB stars (initial masses $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}7\,M_{\odot}$ ) remain poorly constrained [60]. Very long-period Mira variables (periods $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d; VLP Miras hereafter) are extremely rare, potentially because they represent a short-lived phase of stellar evolution [46] or because such long pulsation periods are attained only by the most massive AGB stars [17, 21].

As summarized in Menzies et al. [47], there are less than 20 known Galactic Mira variables in this period range, found very close to the Galactic plane – supporting their association with the most massive AGB stars [82] as predicted by theoretical models [74]. Many of these VLP Miras are also classified as OH/IR stars, which are dust-obscured, oxygen-rich AGB stars exhibiting circumstellar OH maser emission. OH/IR stars can exhibit particularly long pulsation periods and are often associated with higher-mass AGB populations [32, 51]. Extremely long period Miras have also been suggested to hide the long-sought populations of the most massive ( $7-9$ M⊙) ‘super’ AGB stars (SAGB; Siess 61, Doherty et al. 13) that ignite carbon under partially degenerate conditions, producing O–Ne–Mg cores and possibly electron-capture supernovae [73, 58, 29].

Despite their significance, the identification of VLP Miras is difficult. Their location in the dusty Galactic plane, together with intense mass loss that enshrouds them in circumstellar dust, have precluded systematic identification in optical time domain surveys. No unambiguous SAGB star has been identified, largely because their luminosities and mass-loss properties overlap those of massive AGB stars (that have not undergone C-core ignition) and red supergiants [14, 53]. Theoretical models predict that some SAGB stars may exhibit chemical peculiarities in their late evolution [13, 52] due to terminal dredge-up episodes, making them appear distinct from massive AGB stars. Therefore, systematic searches for VLP Miras in infrared (IR) time domain surveys together with spectroscopic characterization to probe chemical composition offer a powerful avenue to search for these elusive end-fates in stellar evolution.

The majority of the known VLP Mira variables are found in targeted surveys of the Large/Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC/SMC) and nearby galaxies. Early near-IR surveys of the LMC and SMC identified only a few dozen such stars [16, 64, 66]. The longest period objects in these samples reach periods $P\approx 2000$ d, and occupy the extreme bright and red end of the AGB sequence [22]. IR surveys such as Surveying the Agents of a Galaxy’s Evolution (SAGE) and Dust in Nearby Galaxies with Spitzer (DUSTiNGS) expanded this population by uncovering numerous dust-enshrouded long-period Miras [57, 56, 8, 7]. The SPitzer InfraRed Intensive Transients Survey (SPIRITS) mid-IR monitoring program [37] revealed objects with periods extending to $\sim 3000$ days in nearby galaxies [35]; however, aliasing remains a limitation with period identification due to the sparse cadence. Due to their faintness at optical/near-IR bands, most sources remain without chemical characterization. Although some sources have probable chemical classifications with low resolution mid-IR spectroscopy or (primarily) photometry [63, 86, 23], higher resolution confirmation is unavailable.

The census of VLP Miras within the Galaxy remains much less well charted, limited by the need for wide-area IR surveys of the Galactic plane. Soszyński et al. [65] and Albarracín et al. [1] presented catalogs of several thousand Galactic Miras towards the Galactic bulge and the far side of the disk from the Optical Gravitaional Lensing Experiment (OGLE; Udalski et al. 76) and Vista Variables in the Via Lactea (VVV; Minniti et al. 49) surveys respectively; however these catalogs did not include any objects with $P>1000$ d either due to different search criteria (e.g., focusing on Galactic kinematics with VVV data) or their red colors (which prevents discovery in the OGLE filters). Suh [67] and Groenewegen [25] presented all-sky catalogs of Galactic Mira variables using data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) surveys [84, 45], finding several dozen Galactic Mira variables with $P>1000$ d. The very slow cadence of NEOWISE also makes identification of the fundamental pulsation periods difficult [67, 68].

Although historically limited, the field of IR stellar time domain astronomy is opening up thanks to synoptic near-IR surveys. These surveys now offer pathways to a systematic census of the longest period objects for detailed chemical characterization. Recently, Suresh et al. [71] presented the first systematic catalog of long-period variables identified from the Palomar Gattini-IR (PGIR) survey [11, 50]. The catalog contains $>150,000$ Long Period Variables identified from $J$ -band light curves, including several hundred with candidate periods $>1000$ d. Utilizing the same dataset, Earley et al. [15] presented a catalog of the largest amplitude variable sources from the PGIR, which identified a number of the longest period Mira variables (owing to their large amplitude fundamental mode pulsations). The high cadence of PGIR ( $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}3$ d) allows us to conclusively identify fundamental mode pulsations, removing the severe contamination from both aliasing and long secondary period variations (see Appendix sec:app; Riebel et al. 57, Riebel et al. 56, Soszyński et al. 64).

Here, we present near-IR spectroscopy of the thirteen VLP Miras confirmed from vetting of PGIR light curves of previously identified candidates – to i) conclusively remove aliasing contaminants, ii) carry out chemical characterization and iii) compare against theoretical expectations for massive AGB evolution predicted by stellar models to understand their nature. Section sec:obs describes the sample selection criteria and spectroscopic observations. In Section sec:analysis, we discuss quantitative estimation of the pulsation periods and classification of their spectroscopic chemistry. Section sec:models compares the derived chemical properties with models of stellar evolution, highlighting one source with peculiar chemistry and possible explanations. We end with a summary and future outlook in Section sec:summary.

## II Observations and Data Reduction

### II.1 Sample Selection

*Figure 1: PGIR $J$ -band light curves for the 13 VLP Mira variables in our sample – black circles indicate observed photometry with error bars, together with the best-fit pulsation period ( $P$ ) and amplitude ( $\Delta J$ ). The red shaded regions include time periods where the source was nominally brighter than the survey saturation limit, and hence the photometry is unreliable. The saturation threshold was increased by $\approx 2$ mag later in the survey due to modified detector readout [10].*

Our targets were selected using data from the PGIR survey, which has monitored the entire visible sky since 2018 with a cadence of $\approx 1{-}3$ nights in $J$ band and a depth of $\approx 15$ Vega mag. The sensitivity, cadence, and increasing baseline ( $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}2500$ d) of PGIR make it especially well suited to identifying long-period, dust obscured, infrared-bright Mira variables that are otherwise invisible even in the deepest optical time domain surveys. To construct our sample of $P\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d Mira variables, we began with the recently published catalog of long-period variables [71]. We down-select this sample to those with reported bestperiod or maxperiod $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d, which yielded 11187 candidates. Since this sample was created using only the first $\approx 1400$ d of PGIR data, most of the reported sources were found to be spurious upon visual inspection of light curves. We therefore used the public light curve catalog [50] together with more recent photometry that provides a total baseline of $\approx 2500$ d.

Because very long period variability is also seen in semi-regular red giants, we visually inspected the light curves to identify sources with bona fide large-amplitude pulsations of i) amplitude $\Delta J\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}2$ mag (removing red giants and long secondary period pulsations that have amplitudes $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}1$ mag; Soszyński et al. 64) and ii) $P\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d, as approximately verified by the peak-to-peak separation (see Section sec:analysis for subsequent quantitative analysis). This produced a sample of 5 sources. Because the catalog in Suresh et al. [71] was created from earlier PGIR data, we also analyzed the recent compilation of large amplitude variables from Earley et al. [15] to select longer period variables. This yielded an additional 2 sources with existing near-IR spectroscopic follow-up.

To complete our sample, we also examined the catalog of the 145 longest period variables with $P>1000$ d identified from NEOWISE data by Groenewegen [25]. Because their sample was created from very slow cadence ( $\approx 6$ month) light curves, we extracted PGIR light curves of all the reported $P\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d sources in their sample within the PGIR footprint, identifying an additional 6 Mira variables that satisfy the same amplitude/period criteria. Details of the sample selection and contaminants are provided in Appendix sec:app. Given that PGIR is limited by confusion in the most crowded Galactic plane fields [11], we expect our sample to be complete for sources with mean brightness of $J\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}12.5$ Vega mag. ### II.2 Spectroscopic Observations

*Figure 2: Near-IR spectra of the 13 targets in our sample (indicated by name), highlighting prominent molecular absorption features used for spectroscopic classification. The gray shaded regions indicate known regions of water absorption bands.*

We carried out near-IR spectroscopic observations of the sources with the 3.0-m NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) on Maunakea during semester 2025A (Program 2025A079; PI: De). We employed the SpeX spectrograph in the short cross-dispersed (SXD) mode, which provides a resolving power of $R\approx 2000$ with the $0.3^{\prime\prime}$ slit and simultaneous coverage of the $0.7{-}2.5\,\mu$ m wavelength range [54]. To achieve S/N $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}50$ across the spectral range, we adopted AB nod sequences with individual exposures of 15 s. Typical sequences consisted of six exposures (ABABAB), giving a total integration time of $\approx 90$ s per target. Flats and arc frames were obtained every 2–4 targets, following standard calibration procedures.

We reduced the data using the pyspextool package22 2 https://github.com/pyspextool/pyspextool [9], which performs flat-fielding, wavelength calibration, sky subtraction, and optimal spectral extraction. Wavelength calibration was achieved using internal arc lamps, while telluric correction was performed using observations of nearby A0V stars at similar airmass to each science target. The final spectra were flux calibrated using telluric standards. The new spectra were supplemented with previously published spectra of sources from the catalog of Earley et al. [15]. Our final sample of spectra includes all 13 VLP Mira variables with $P\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d; their broadband spectra are shown in Figure fig:fullspec.

## III Analysis

### III.1 Period Estimation

The well-sampled $J$ -band light curves of the sources are shown in Figure fig:sample. Nearly all of these sources are not detected in contemporaneous optical surveys (such as the Zwicky Transient Facility; Bellm et al. 4) due to their extremely red colors. The light curves predominantly show a primary, large amplitude ( $\Delta J\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}2.0$ mag) pulsation mode; in a few cases superimposed with higher frequency variability. We use a semi-parametric Gaussian process regression model including a fundamental mode pulsation, a higher frequency overtone and a long-term trend [27] to derive the fundamental pulsation period. We use the R code distributed by He et al. [27] to derive a primary pulsation period from the log-likelihood periodogram and a best-fit $J$ -band light curve model including higher frequency variability terms. We estimate the statistical uncertainty in the period by simulating 10 realizations of the observed light curve by adding Gaussian noise scaled to the photometric uncertainties.

### III.2 Spectroscopic classification

*Figure 3: Continuum-normalized spectra of the sample of VLP Miras together with reference objects from the IRTF Spectral Library (HD 31996 and IRAS 01037+1219). Strong atomic and molecular absorption features are marked. For both the sample and reference objects, we indicate O-rich spectral types with blue/navy blue colors, and C-rich types with red/brown colors.*

All of the sample sources exhibit red continua, commonly marked by inverted V-shaped broad absorption feature expected from water molecules. The only exception is IRAS 19552+3142, which exhibits a steep red continuum with no observable water absorption. To highlight the weaker features on top of the continuum, we show their continuum normalized spectra in Figure fig:specnorm. We classified the 13 targets into O-rich or C-rich chemistry by identifying diagnostic molecular absorption features in the SpeX spectra using well-established spectroscopic indicators [55, 48] for evolved AGB stars. All sources except one (IRAS 19552+3142) exhibit O-rich chemistry – with dominant Titanium Oxide (TiO) bandheads in the $J$ band and deep water vapor (H2O) absorption troughs at $1.4\,\mu$ m and $1.9\,\mu$ m (Figure fig:fullspec). All sources exhibit deep CO first overtone absorption in $K$ -band, characteristic of AGB spectra [55].

The continuum normalized spectra exhibit more subtle differences between the spectra: three O-rich sources (IRAS 17501-2656, IRAS 18176-1848 and IRAS 18560+0638) show clear absorption bandheads of AlO in the $H$ -band, and one source (IRAS 18585+0900) also exhibits noticeable $H$ -band absorption band-heads of the CO second overtone. AlO is a rare molecule in astrophysical environments, but has been shown to be relatively common in AGB stars at very low temperatures and O-rich environments [3] – confirming the highly evolved nature of these sources. Two sources (IRAS 07222-2005 and IRAS 19508+2659) exhibit weak emission lines of H, e.g., Pa- $\beta$ near $1.28\,\mu$ m and the Br series, commonly seen in pulsating Mira variables due to shocks in their extended atmospheres [72, 31]. IRAS 19552+3142 is an outlier, exhibiting clear C-rich chemistry: it lacks continuum water absorption and other O-rich molecules; instead it only exhibits a clear C2 absorption bandhead at $\approx 1.75\,\mu$ m. Next, we compare the observed chemical properties to stellar evolution models in Section sec:models, paying specific attention to the peculiar C-rich object.

## IV Stellar evolution models

### IV.1 Comparison to model grids

We leverage existing stellar evolution models to compare the results of our chemical characterization against stellar theory. Past theoretical works make predictions for the evolution of periods of Mira variables as a function of initial mass and age – with the surface chemistry being modified over time due to dredge-up episodes from the stellar interior. In general, stars with lower initial masses ( $M_{i}\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}2$ M⊙) ascend the AGB without significant alteration of their surface chemistry [80]. Therefore, they are predicted to evolve into relatively short period Miras ( $P\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}300$ d) with surface chemistry close to solar composition ( $C/O\approx 0.6$ , producing O-rich chemistry). As more massive stars ( $2$ M⊙ $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}M_{i}\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$<$}}}4$ M⊙) attain higher luminosities (and larger radii) in AGB evolution, strong mixing episodes due to the third dredge-up (TDU) are predicted to strongly enhance C-fraction at the surface producing C-rich Miras at periods reaching $\approx 500-600$ d. For even more massive AGB stars, the effect of TDU is nullified due to the even higher core temperatures that are predicted to destroy the synthesized C via the CNO cycle (hot-bottom burning or HBB; Herwig 28), leading to the most massive AGB stars ( $M_{i}\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}4$ M⊙) attaining the longest periods ( $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d) with O-rich composition.

*Figure 4: Theoretical predictions for the evolution of pulsation period with surface chemistry for Mira variables at different initial masses (see legend) from the models of Trabucchi et al. [74], Trabucchi et al. [75] (T21) and the terminal models of Vassiliadis and Wood [79] (V93). For comparison we overlay the pulsation periods of our sample with their inferred surface chemistry (C/O $<1$ for O-rich and C/O $>1$ for C-rich).*

We summarize the expected evolution in Figure fig:period_co, plotting the predicted Mira fundamental pulsation period as a function of surface chemistry. We generated isochrones using the CMD v3.9 interface33 3 https://stev.oapd.inaf.it/cgi-bin/cmd_3.9, utilizing PARSEC v1.2S tracks integrated with COLIBRI thermally pulsing AGB models [46]. The models incorporate standard circumstellar dust and mass loss prescriptions, with pulsation periods (fundamental mode, pmode=0) computed using the methods described in Trabucchi et al. [74], Trabucchi et al. [75]. In all cases, the stars evolve to increasingly longer pulsation periods during their evolution before mass loss terminates the AGB phase. The longest periods ( $\approx 1000$ d) are achieved for the most massive stars with $M_{i}\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}6$ M⊙with O-rich surface composition. On the other hand, C-rich Miras arise in a mass range of $2-4$ M⊙(for solar metallicity), reaching maximum periods of $\approx 600$ d. For comparison, we also overlay the terminal pulsation period and C/O as a function of initial mass from the earlier solar metallicity models of Vassiliadis and Wood [79]. These models reach even longer periods of $\approx 2800$ d with O-rich composition for massive AGB stars, although they do not reproduce C-rich chemistry at solar metallicity.

To compare our results to this suite, we also overlay the pulsation period and inferred surface composition for our VLP Miras; we employ approximate estimates for the C/O ratio based on the identified spectral features. As shown, the O-rich stars in our sample occupy the expected region for the longest period Mira variables expected from theoretical models. As such, these objects serve as a signpost for the most massive AGB stars currently in the Milky Way undergoing the TP-AGB phase. However, the peculiar C-type object IRAS 19552+3142 is not explained by these models, with a pulsation period more than twice as long as the longest periods expected at C-rich chemistry. Its exceptionally long period may indicate a very large radius and, in turn, very high luminosity that is akin to the most massive AGB stars – that has peculiarly turned C-rich in its terminal phase. In the next section, we further examine the C-rich candidate via modeling of its spectral energy distribution (SED) to estimate its physical properties.

We carry out a closer examination of the C-rich IRAS 19552+314244 4 The source was previously identified as a C-star in Suh [68] based on WISE data but its pulsation period was incorrect. to estimate its stellar and circumstellar properties. The source has prior near-IR photometry from the Two Micron All-sky Survey (2MASS; [62]), WISE [84] as well as low resolution spectroscopy spanning $\approx 8-24\,\mu$ m from the IRAS mission [42]. We compile these measurements and show their SED in Figure fig:seds; we caution that the large variability of the source (Figure fig:sample) makes it difficult to interpret SEDs compiled from multiple surveys. The source exhibits a steep red SED peaking at $\approx 5\,\mu$ m, together with a clear emission feature in its IRAS spectrum near $\approx 11\,\mu$ m55 5 We do not correct the near-IR photometry for interstellar extinction since the total flux output is dominated by flux at $>2\,\mu$ m, given uncertainties with variability due to pulsation phase and interstellar dust models. Both O-rich silicate molecules and C-rich SiC molecules have emission features in this region; Little-Marenin et al. [44] previously associated this feature with SiC, suggesting a C-star classification [68]. We carry out a closer comparison of the observed SED with radiative transfer models to constrain the circumstellar environment.

Ventura et al. [81] presented a sample of IR SED models for C-rich and O-rich AGB stars of $\approx 1.5$ M⊙and $\approx 5.0$ M⊙. Although nominally constructed for lower mass AGB stars, the IR SED is sensitive primarily to the circumstellar chemistry and therefore their grid of SEDs as a function of optical depth (at $10\,\mu$ m; $\tau_{10}$ ) is useful for comparison (as higher mass primarily increases the bolometric luminosity). Figure fig:seds shows a comparison of the SED of IRAS 19552+3142 to these models; both types of chemistry produce an observable feature around $\approx 11\,\mu$ m. While the steep red color is matched by the higher $\tau_{10}$ model in the O-rich case, both O-rich models produce a prominent emission feature at $\approx 18\,\mu$ m not observed in the data. The C-rich models at $\tau_{10}\approx 1$ reproduce the weak emission feature at $\approx 11\,\mu$ m, the featureless slope between $12-20\,\mu$ m as well as the red color, confirming a C-rich circumstellar dust envelope.

We can translate the observed SED and inferred optical depth of the dust into physical parameters for the star. Integrating the observed SED of the source between $1-30\,\mu$ m, we estimate a bolometric flux of $\approx 2.2\times 10^{-8}$ erg cm-2 s-1. However, since their distance estimation method was calibrated for O-rich LPVs, and adopting this distance would not affect our conclusions, and we retain the distance estimate from Bailer-Jones et al. [2]. of $\approx 5.5^{+2.0}_{-2.1}$ kpc (using the geometric distance estimate of Bailer-Jones et al. 2, since these extremely red objects have anomalous colors for photo-geometric estimates). Therefore, we estimate the $1-30\,\mu$ m luminosity of the source to be $\approx(1-4)\times 10^{4}$ L⊙. Assuming a stellar temperature of $\approx 2500$ K expected for extremely cool AGB stars [69], the corresponding stellar radius is $R_{*}\approx 500-1000$ R⊙. $$ \begin{split}\dot{M}\approx{}&10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr^{-1}}\left(\tau_{10}\right)\left(\frac{550\,{\rm cm^{2}\,g^{-1}}}{\kappa_{10}}\right)\\
&\times\left(\frac{R_{\rm in}}{1.5\times 10^{14}\,{\rm cm}}\right)\left(\frac{v_{d}}{15\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}}\right)\left(\frac{10^{-3}}{r_{dg}}\right)\end{split} $$

where $\kappa_{10}$ is the dust opacity (per unit dust mass; Zubko et al. 87) at $10\,\mu$ m, $R_{in}$ is the inner radius of the dust shell (assumed to be at $\approx 2-5\times R_{*}$ ), $v_{d}$ is the wind velocity and $r_{dg}$ is the dust to gas mass ratio77 7 We note that uncertainties in the dust to gas ratio may introduce order unity corrections in the inferred mass loss rate.

### IV.3 The nature of IRAS 19552+3142

Motivated by the combination of the long pulsation period ( $\approx 1060$ d) and peculiar C-rich composition of IRAS 19552+3142, our modeling reveals the following characteristics: i) the C-rich photospheric composition is accompanied by an extended C-rich dust shell, ii) a high luminosity in the range $\approx(1-4)\times 10^{4}$ L⊙and iii) an elevated mass loss rate $\sim 10^{-4}$ M⊙ yr-1. For comparison, distance estimates for a subset of the O-rich VLP Miras from Bhattacharya et al. [6] place them in the relatively nearby Galactic disk, with luminosities broadly comparable to that of IRAS 19552+3142 (see also Figure fig:seds). Despite these similarities, their contrasting chemistry remain difficult to reconcile with the models discussed above, in which stars reaching the longest periods remain O-rich as HBB prevents C dredge-up.

We attempt to understand its nature by drawing comparisons to both previously observed objects and theoretical models. IRAS 19552+3142 shares some similarities to the class of objects known as the luminous carbon stars in the Magellanic Clouds [78]. Their proposed explanation is that mass loss reduces the envelope mass until HBB ceases, allowing further TDU episodes to make the star carbon-rich before it leaves the AGB. The brightest object in that study, IRAS 04496-6958, has a C-rich atmosphere but retains an O-rich dust component, consistent with the cessation of an earlier O-rich wind. IRAS 19552+3142 instead shows carbon-rich chemistry in both its atmosphere and the dust traced by its mid-IR spectrum – indicating a relatively long-lived ( $\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}10^{4}$ yr) HBB turn-off phase. However, should HBB turn-off be universal in the late-phase evolution of the most luminous (and longest period) VLP Miras, we would expect to see a higher fraction of C-rich VLP Miras; instead, 12 of our 13 VLP Miras are O-rich, suggesting that any late HBB turn-off phase has to be restricted to a subset of these stars. Further theoretical work is therefore needed to confirm the duration of the HBB turn-off and if it can produce luminous stars with both C-rich photosphere and circumstellar dust.

An alternative explanation is that the long period reflects envelope expansion rather than a particularly high initial mass. Dell’Agli et al. [12] suggested that common-envelope (CE) interaction with an engulfed companion could explain the large radii and high mass-loss rates of extremely red carbon stars in the Magellanic Clouds [26]. In this picture, the rise in molecular opacity after C/O exceeds unity may expand the star, potentially initiating interaction with a companion, and explaining both the large radius and strong mass loss inferred for IRAS 19552+3142. This model is likely inconsistent for two reasons.

First, Figure fig:seds compares our sources with LMC Mira variables and OH masers [57], and the long-period variables from the SPIRITS survey [35]. We also show the region occupied by the extreme AGB star progenitors of intermediate luminosity red transients, as defined by Thompson et al. [73]. Most of our sources fall within this region given their distance and color uncertainties, despite having different chemistries. Thus, these extreme colors and luminosities do not require a transition to C-rich chemistry, and therefore binary interaction driven by C-opacity expansion is not a prerequisite to producing very long period red objects. Second, the longest-period C-rich Galactic88 8 Groenewegen and Sloan [23] provide a list of 5 C-rich Mira variables in the LMC with $P>1000$ d; however some of these may be unreliable since some periods come from low-cadence NEOWISE data (e.g., Appendix sec:app) and uncertain color-based chemical classification for very red objects [47]. Mira variable previously reported in the literature has a pulsation period99 9 The Galactic source V0829 Cas has been suggested as a C-Mira with a period of 1060 d [24] but its classification remains unclear due to lack of available details [18]. of 725 d [43]. IRAS 19552+3142 would therefore represent the longest-period (by $>50$ %) C-rich AGB star identified in the Milky Way. The lack of known stars in this period gap1010 10 Since Mira variables become particularly dust enshrouded only at the longest periods, we suggest that objects with $P<1000$ d are likely more complete in past optical characterization efforts is problematic for the CE interpretation, since we would expect it to be populated by systems spanning a range of binary separations and periods. Therefore, IRAS 19552+3142 possibly represents a distinct, rare evolutionary chain for forming C-stars at extremely long periods.

Finally, we suggest the possibility that IRAS 19552+3142 is an SAGB star that has ignited carbon in its core. Because very massive AGB stars are expected to undergo HBB that prevents dredge-up of C in the TP-AGB phase, SAGB evolution offers an alternative pathway to produce C-rich surface chemistry in prior evolution. Before the thermally pulsing phase, some massive SAGB models undergo dredge-out: a helium-burning convective region meets the hydrogen-rich convective envelope [34], thereby mixing freshly produced carbon to the surface [14]. While subsequent HBB destroys carbon, the star remains C-rich due to the enhancement prior to the TP-AGB phase. This mechanism has been suggested to be a possible explanation for some C-rich extremely metal poor stars with enhancement of s-process elements [34] as well as possible pre-SAGB stars in the Magellanic Clouds [53, 52].

A close analog of IRAS 19552+3142 may be the extreme AGB star MSX SMC 055 (IRAS 00483-7347) in the SMC (see also Kastner et al. 39 for possible candidate in the LMC). This source was previously classified as a large amplitude C-rich star [41] based on optical and Spitzer/IRS spectra, and subsequently shown to be a very long-period, luminous Mira variable ( $P\approx 1800$ d; Groenewegen et al. 22, Groenewegen and Sloan 23) with directly measured enhancement of Rb [20], indicating activation of the s-process and a possible SAGB nature. While this channel may naturally explain the C-rich atmosphere and circumstellar dust in IRAS 19552+31421111 11 The extremely red SED of IRAS 19552+3142 makes it very challenging to obtain a Rb measurement at 7800 Å., we note that this source is likely less luminous but more dust-obscured than MSX SMC 055, indicating a lower mass or earlier phase of evolution. The universality of this phase and its dependence on mass and metallicity therefore require further theoretical investigation [33, 13]; as the only Galactic analog of MSX SMC 055, future detailed studies of IRAS 19552+3142 would be crucial to understand its circumstellar environment (e.g. via radio maser lines).

The possible SAGB origin is also supported by the progenitors of intermediate-luminosity red transients, which have been proposed to be electron-capture supernovae from SAGB progenitors (also known as SN 2008S-like transients; Hiramatsu et al. 29, Thompson et al. 73), and the progenitors of some nearby Type-II supernovae from low-mass supergiant progenitors. Late-time JWST spectroscopy of AT 2019abn revealed Class C PAH features indicating carbonaceous circumstellar material [58]. Similarly, Kilpatrick et al. [40] reported the detection of graphitic dust1212 12 See also Van Dyk et al. [77] who claimed O-rich dust around the progenitor of SN 2025pht. around the progenitor of the Type II SN 2025pht – indicating a massive star ( $\approx 15$ M⊙) surrounded by C-rich circumstellar medium. IRAS 19552+3142 shares this broad chemical property and lies in the color-magnitude region associated with SN 2008S-like progenitors (Figure fig:seds), although its colors are substantially bluer than the progenitor of SN 2025pht. Its high inferred mass-loss rate is also consistent with a heavily obscured progenitor – suggesting the presence of a common mechanism that likely substantially enhances the terminal mass loss rate for all these sources.

## V Summary and Future Prospects

We combined long-baseline PGIR photometry with near-IR spectroscopy from IRTF to identify and characterize Galactic very long period Mira variables that have historically remained out of the reach of optical time domain surveys. Our main results are:

- • We confirmed 13 large-amplitude Mira variables with pulsation periods $P\mathrel{\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{\lower 4.0pt\hbox{$\sim$}}\hss}\hbox{$>$}}}1000$ d. The dense cadence and $\approx 2500$ d baseline of PGIR allow us to distinguish genuine long-period pulsations from aliases and spurious periods in earlier catalogs.

- • Twelve of the thirteen sources exhibit O-rich spectra, with prominent H2O and TiO absorption. Their long periods and surface chemistry are broadly consistent with massive AGB stars undergoing hot-bottom burning. Several also show AlO absorption or hydrogen emission associated with their cool, pulsating atmospheres.

- • IRAS 19552+3142 is the sole C-rich source, with a pulsation period of $\approx 1060$ d, making it the longest-period C-rich AGB star identified in the Milky Way to date. It exhibits photospheric C2 absorption, while its mid-IR spectrum independently supports carbon-rich circumstellar dust, including SiC emission near $11.3\,\mu$ m. This combination is not reproduced by the standard AGB model grids available in the literature.

- • The SED and plausible distance range of IRAS 19552+3142 imply a luminosity of $\approx(1-4)\times 10^{4}$ L⊙, a radius of $\approx 500-1000$ R⊙, and a mass-loss rate of order $10^{-4}$ M⊙ yr-1 under the adopted wind and dust assumptions. These estimates remain limited by the uncertain distance, but nonetheless confirm a heavily enshrouded, luminous AGB star with C-rich chemistry.

- • We discuss possible explanations for IRAS 19552+3142 – including a late carbon-rich phase following the cessation of HBB and envelope expansion enhanced by binary interaction. Neither scenario readily explains why most stars in our sample are O-rich or why VLP C-rich Miras are so rare. These mechanisms must therefore operate in only a small fraction of stars.

- • Instead, we discuss the possibility of a SAGB progenitor involving dredge-out before the TP-AGB phase, resulting in C-rich surface chemistry even if HBB prevents further enrichment of C. Its chemistry and circumstellar properties make it an interesting analog of dust-obscured transient progenitors. Improved luminosity and abundance measurements, together with predictions for the duration of these phases, are needed to distinguish these possibilities.

A more complete census requires cadenced IR time-domain surveys spanning multiple pulsation cycles, coupled with spectroscopy to establish surface and circumstellar chemistry. Many additional VLP Miras likely remain undetected toward the Galactic bulge, where source confusion limits PGIR sensitivity and therefore a census of their total numbers. Current surveys such as the PRime-focus Infrared Microlensing Experiment (PRIME; Sumi et al. 70) will be particularly well suited to finding and monitoring this population over a long baseline in a high metallicity environment. Similarly, the upcoming Cryoscope project will complete the census of these bright IR variables in the southern Milky Way [38]. Although similarly luminous Galactic sources will generally saturate surveys with the Roman Space Telescope, their extragalactic counterparts offer a promising route to measuring the incidence of these rare phases and clarifying the final evolution of massive AGB and SAGB stars. In particular, Roman surveys of nearby galaxies will extend these searches to populations with well-constrained distances, complemented by JWST mid-IR spectroscopy to establish the photospheric and circumstellar chemistry.

## Appendix A Sample selection and contaminants

Groenewegen [25] provides a recent summary of the sample of VLP Mira variables known in the Milky Way. The previous largest list was cataloged in Menzies et al. [47], who reported a sample of 17 Galactic sources with $P>1000$ d. Nearly all of these sources do not have previously reported near-IR spectroscopy; however, we focus our work on objects where the periods can be confirmed with PGIR data. 16 of these sources lie within the PGIR observing footprint, while only 4 are sufficiently bright in $J$ -band for reliable PGIR light curves in crowded Galactic fields. We verified the periods of these objects, and included these objects in our sample (2 of these were already included based on the compilation from Suresh et al. 71 and Earley et al. 15).

Groenewegen [25] presented a sample of 154 VLP Mira candidates based on NEOWISE time series. However, the slow cadence of the NEOWISE survey and the severe saturation for these bright mid-IR sources requires re-examination of the claimed periodicities with PGIR light curves (where possible). We generated $J$ -band light curves of 78 sources that fall within the PGIR observing footprint – while most of these sources are too faint in $J$ -band for photometric measurements, we find significant contamination of this sample with objects that have clearly shorter periods. Figure fig:contam shows examples where the ground-based, higher cadence data clearly indicate shorter period variability. Of the 19 sources with reliable PGIR time series, 9 have $P>1000$ d; 3 of these 9 sources were already included in our sample based on the Menzies et al. [47] and Suresh et al. [71] catalog, resulting in the addition of 6 new sources. We also investigated the reported three C-Miras with $P>1000$ d (identified from WISE light curves) in Suh [68]: one of the three sources (IRAS 16328-4656) lies outside the PGIR footprint, one is too faint in near-IR (the unconfirmed V0829 Cas reported in Groenewegen et al. 24) while one object (RAFGL 996) clearly shows shorter timescale pulsations in its PGIR light curves reported in Earley et al. ## Abstract

We present the luminosity function and volumetric rate of a sample of Type IIP supernovae (SNe) from the Zwicky Transient Facility Census of the Local Universe survey (CLU). This is the largest sample of Type IIP SNe from a systematic volume-limited survey to-date. The final sample includes 330 Type IIP SNe and 36 low-luminosity Type II (LLIIP) SNe with $M_{\textrm{r,peak}}>-16$ mag, which triples the literature sample of LLIIP SNe. The fraction of LLIIP SNe is $19^{+3}_{-4}\%$ of the total CLU Type IIP SNe population ( $8^{+1}_{-2}\%$ of all core-collapse SNe). This implies that while LLIIP SNe likely represent the fate of core-collapse SNe of $8-12$ $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ progenitors, they alone cannot account for the fate of all massive stars in this mass range. To derive an absolute rate, we estimate the ZTF pipeline efficiency as a function of the apparent magnitude and the local surface brightness. We derive a volumetric rate of $(3.9_{-0.4}^{+0.4})\times 10^{4}\ \textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for Type IIP SNe and $(7.3_{-0.6}^{+0.6})\times 10^{3}\ \textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for LLIIP SNe. Now that the rate of LLIIP SNe is robustly derived, the unresolved discrepancy between core-collapse SN rates and star-formation rates cannot be explained by LLIIP SNe alone.

## I Introduction

Core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), the explosive endpoints of massive stars, drive chemical evolution in galaxies, provide impetus for the formation of new generations of stars, and leave behind neutron star or black hole remnants. Despite the discovery of over 10,000 SNe, the fate of stars at the low-mass end of CCSNe, with progenitor initial masses of $\approx 8$ –12 $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ , is not well understood [50, 107, e.g., see]. Exploring this mass range is important, because it probes the boundary between whether a star has a large enough mass to form a neutron star from its central core or, instead, leaves behind a white dwarf. Also, it is uncertain whether stars in this mass range undergo iron core-collapse from Red Supergiants (RSG) or if electron capture in super-Asymptotic Giant Branch (sAGB) stars drives the SN explosions [79, 53, 61, 59].

Stars in the $8–12$ $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ range exhibit a distinctly different core structure compared to those with higher progenitor mass, characterized by significantly lower compactness [107]. The evolution of such stars is more complex to model than at $>12$ $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ due to the development of thermal pulses that are numerically challenging to follow, and highly uncertain late-time mass-loss [74, 118, e.g.,]. The lowest mass CCSNe have steep density gradients outside their degenerate cores, liberate less gravitational binding energy, have lower neutrino luminosities, and ultimately are associated with lower luminosities, explosion energy and nickel yield [50, 77, 14, 32, 105, 13, 98, 4, 15].

It is critical to understand this faint end of the core-collapse luminosity function, constrain their rates and couple the stellar evolution initial mass function (IMF) to the known SN populations. Determining the SN rate and tying it to the mass boundary between stars that do and do not explode as SNe is vital for determining the number of neutron stars, galactic chemical evolution and dust evolution models, and the total energy released by SNe into the environment. The CCSN distribution traces the formation of massive stars and the CCSN rate should match the massive star formation rate using the known star-formation rate density and IMF, given our current understanding of stellar evolution. However, there is an apparent discrepancy between the two absolute rates with the star-formation implying a much higher CCSN rate than is observed. This ongoing debate has been discussed extensively in the literature [45, 12, 44, 17, 119, 52, e.g.,]. One possibility is that this disagreement arises from a missing population of low-luminosity CCSNe.

One such class of faint CCSNe is low-luminosity Type IIP SNe (LLIIP SNe), which likely represent the explosions of $8-12$ $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ progenitor stars. LLIIP SNe exhibit a faint peak luminosity, defined here as $M_{\textrm{r,peak}}\geq-16$ mag, motivated by prior literature [104, e.g.,]. Recent studies, based on pre-explosion images of SNe 2005cs, 2008bk, 2018aoq, 2022acko [72, 63, 69, 82, 117] also show that SNe with $r$ -band peak $>-16$ mag have progenitor mass estimates less than 11 $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ , while those with brighter peak have progenitor masses $>$ 12 M☉(see Figure 12 in Appendix A). The nickel mass ( $\sim 0.005$ M☉) of LLIIP SNe is an order of magnitude lower than that typically found in standard Type II SNe [92, e.g.,]. Additionally, LLIIP SNe are characterized by slow expansion velocities (approximately 1300 $-$ 2500 km s-1 at 50 days after the explosion), indicating low explosion energies. The low energy and low nickel mass could be explained by the explosion of $8-12$ M☉ progenitors. This is also favored by lightcurve simulations [88, 36], evolutionary numerical simulations of low mass RSGs [64], and nebular spectroscopy [53]. A correlation is also observed between the explosion energy, nickel mass and progenitor mass estimates from pre-SN imaging [32], where lower-mass progenitors ( $<12$ $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ ) are associated with lower nickel mass ( $<0.01$ M☉) and lower explosion energy ( $<2\times 10^{50}$ erg s-1).

However, there are only about a dozen such objects presented in the literature [112, 104, 49, 78, 89, 120, 114, 60, 10, 109, 26]. For a Salpeter IMF [95], around 50% of the potential CCSN progenitors reside in the $8-12$ $\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ mass range. Given this fact, it is surprising that such SNe are rarely detected. What do half of the stars that undergo core-collapse explode as? It is likely that this deficit of discovery can be explained by the connection between these relatively low-mass progenitors and the occurrence of low-luminosity SNe, which are more difficult to detect and classify.

In this series of three papers, we present the analysis of a sample of 36 LLIIP SNe detected by Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) as part of the Census of the Local Universe (CLU) Survey, which roughly triples the number of existing LLIIP SNe in the literature. The focus of the first paper is to estimate their luminosity function and volumetric rates.

To place these results in a broader context, we also present a sample of 330 Type IIP SNe, obtained from the largest systematic volume-limited SN survey to date. The previous Type II SNe sample from a volume-limited sample survey includes 62 Type II SNe from the Lick Observatory Supernova Search [62, LOSS;]. Other Type II samples from systematics surveys include 50 Type II SNe from the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System [97, PS1;], 34 Type IIP SNe from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey II Supernova Survey [108, SDSS-II SNS;] and 21 Type II SNe from the Caltech Core-collapse SN Project [3, CCCP;].

In Section II.2, we define the sample selection criteria. The data obtained and the extinction correction method are described in Sections III and IV, respectively. In Sections V and VI, we estimate the luminosity function and the volumetric rate of LLIIP SNe and compare with the overall CLU Type IIP SN population. We discuss the implications of the measured LLIIP rates in Section VII and conclude in Section VIII. In companion Papers II and III, we will present the analysis of their lightcurves and nebular spectra, respectively.

## II Sample Selection

### II.1 Census of the Local Universe

ZTF conducts an optical time-domain survey with the 48-inch Schmidt telescope (P48) situated at Palomar Observatory [7, 40, 29]. The ZTF Census of the Local Universe (CLU) experiment aims to build a comprehensive spectroscopic sample of transients in the local Universe. To accomplish this, we match the hosts of these transients with the galaxy catalog from the Census of the Local Universe [19]. This catalog contains around 234,500 galaxies with established distances, compiled from pre-existing spectroscopic galaxy surveys and the CLU-H $\alpha$ survey (refer to Cook et al. 19 for further details).

The CLU experiment is designed as a volume-limited SN survey where sources at less than 150 Mpc ( $z\leq 0.033$ ) and spatially coincident with (within 30 kpc) or visibly associated with a galaxy in the CLU catalog were assigned for spectroscopic follow-up for classification. For more detailed discussion of the CLU experiment filtering, see De et al. [28]. The filter is implemented on the Global Relay of Observatories Watching Transients Happen (GROWTH) Marshal [55] and the Fritz Marshal [115, 20], both of which are web portals designed for vetting and coordinating transient follow-up observations.

After passing through the CLU filter, the transients are allocated for spectroscopic classification using: the Spectral Energy Distribution Machine [8, 56, SEDM;] at the Palomar 60-inch telescope, the Double-Beam Spectrograph [81, DBSP;] at the Palomar 200-inch Hale telescope, and the Low-Resolution Imaging Spectrometer [80, LRIS;]. In this paper, we consider SNe saved to the CLU experiment starting from 1 October 2018 until 1 April 2024. We exclude the targets saved to ZTF in 2020 as the CLU experiment was inactive during that year. A total of 1745 SNe saved to CLU were classified during this interval.

### II.2 Sample of LLIIP SNe

We apply the following selection criteria on the ZTF SN sample obtained from the CLU survey:

- 1. Type II Classification: From the CLU sample, 727 candidates classified as Type II (including subtypes IIP, II, IIL, II-norm, and II-pec) were selected.

- 2. Peak Magnitude: A Gaussian process fit was applied to the forced photometry light curves, and the sample was restricted to those with a peak magnitude $m_{peak_{r}}<20$ mag, resulting in 719 candidates. The peak magnitude and other lightcurve parameters are measured on this GP fit (see Section III.1 for details.). The 20 mag cut is chosen as the pipeline recovery efficiency and classification completeness drops below 80% for alerts fainter than 20 mag (see Section V).

- 3. In order to constrain the $r$ -band peak, we first require that the candidates have more than 10 detections, reducing the sample to 626. We also require that the candidates pass any one of the following conditions: (a) Candidates with at least one detection before the peak and one after the peak, and for which the duration between the last non-detection and the first detection ( $t_{firstdet}-t_{lastnon-det}$ ) was $\leq 20$ days. (b) If $t_{firstdet}-t_{lastnon-det}\geq 20$ days, then candidates with more than 10 pre-peak detections and more than 2 post-peak detections, as well as a magnitude difference $mag_{firstdet}-mag_{peak}>1$ mag, were considered. (c) For candidates where the first detection corresponds to the peak, the last non-detection had to occur within 10 days of the first detection. 394 candidates pass this quality cut.

- 4. Plateau Criterion: Candidates were required to show a plateau phase, defined as a duration of $\geq$ 40 days with a drop of less than 1 magnitude, resulting in a sample of 330 candidates.

- 5. Peak Absolute Magnitude: To obtain the absolute magnitudes, we use the distance modulus calculated from the host redshift assuming a cosmological model with $\Omega_{M}=0.3$ , $\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7$ , and $h=0.7$ . For galaxies closer than 25 Mpc, we correct for the Virgo, Great Attractor, and Shapley supercluster infall based on the NASA Extragalactic Database object page [41, NED11 1 https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/;]. We ignore corrections due to peculiar motions for galaxies farther than 25 Mpc. If the peculiar motion of the galaxy is $\sim 300$ km s-1, then the error of the peak magnitude is $\leq 0.1$ mag. Table A lists the distances used for the nearby galaxies and their references. We apply a K-correction of $2.5\times$ log(1 + z) for all the SNe in our sample. The LLIIP sample is restricted to those with a peak absolute magnitude less luminous than $-16$ mag, leaving 48 LLIIP SN candidates.

- 6. Host Extinction Correction: Finally, after correcting for host galaxy extinction (see Section IV for details), 36 LLIIP SNe remained in the final sample.

The summary of the selection criteria and the sample are provided in Tables 1 and 2 respectively. The distribution of the number of SNe as a function of peak absolute magnitude is shown in Figure 2. A complementary ZTF experiment is the magnitude-limited Bright Transient Survey [39, 84, BTS;], aimed at classifying transients brighter than a peak apparent magnitude of 18.5 mag without any redshift cut. 62 SNe in our sample are also part of the Type II SN sample of the BTS survey (Y. ## III Data

In this section, we describe the photometric and spectroscopic data used.

### III.1 Optical photometry

We perform forced point-spread function photometry on the ZTF difference images at the location of these SNe using the ZTF forced-photometry service developed by Masci et al. [66], Masci et al. [67] in $g$ and $r$ bands. For this work, we consider anything less than a 3 $\sigma$ detection an upper limit. We used a Gaussian Process (GP) algorithm22 2 https://george.readthedocs.io/ [2] to interpolate the photometric measurements and measure the slope. Figure 1 shows the lightcurves of SNe 2023wcr and 2024wcs as examples. The vertical dashed red line shows the epoch of first detection, and the vertical dashed grey line shows the epoch of last non-detection. The explosion epoch is defined to be midway between the epoch of first detection and last non-detection. The epochs of peak $r$ - and $g$ -band magnitudes are shown by the vertical solid red and blue lines. The photometry data, lightcurve plots, and spectroscopy of all SNe in the sample will be made available on WISEREP and Zenodo after publication.

### III.2 Optical spectroscopy

For each transient, at least one spectrum is usually obtained close to the peak luminosity to establish a spectroscopic classification as described in Section II.1. We employ the SuperNova Identification [9, SNID;] code for these classifications. For spectra that show host galaxy contamination, we utilize superfit [46]. The reduction of DBSP spectra follows the procedures outlined in Bellm and Sesar [6] and Roberson et al. [91], while the SEDM data reductions are detailed in Rigault et al. [90]. The LRIS spectra were reduced using the automated lpipe [83] pipeline.

We also make use of spectra from the Alhambra Faint Object Spectrograph and Camera at the Nordic Optical Telescope [30, NOT;] and from the Spectrograph for the Rapid Acquisition of Transients [85, SPRAT;] on the Liverpool Telescope. The NOT data reduction utilized the PyNOT33 3 https://github.com/jkrogager/PyNOT and PypeIt [87] pipelines. The SPRAT data is processed using a pipeline based on FrodoSpec [5].

## IV Extinction Correction

Extinction is divided into two components: the first component represents dust extinction from the Milky Way, while the second component accounts for extinction originating from the host galaxies of the SNe. To correct for Galactic extinction, we employ the reddening maps provided by Schlafly and Finkbeiner [100], the extinction law described by Cardelli et al. [18] and a value of $R_{V}=3.1$ .

To estimate the host-galaxy extinction, we use the average $g-r$ color curve of the sample. First, we measure the Na I D absorption lines of the host environment [86, 106] when a high SNR SN spectrum is available. To measure the template $g-r$ color, we discard objects with Na I D EW $>$ 1 Å. The 1 $\sigma$ scatter is 0.35 mag. The average color and standard deviation (1 $\sigma$ range) are shown by the black solid line and blue shaded region, respectively, in Figure 3. This template is available on Zenodo. We then measure the $A_{\textrm{V,host}}$ assuming that the SN color exceeding the 1 $\sigma$ $g-r$ template is caused by host extinction. 80 out of the 330 Type IIP SNe has $A_{\textrm{V,host}}>0$ . The sample color curve after this correction is shown in the right panel of Figure 3. The remaining 1 $\sigma$ scatter in the $g-r$ color is likely due to intrinsic properties of the SNe, which could be dominated by photospheric temperature differences [27, e.g., see]. Table 2 lists the measured $A_{\textrm{V,host}}$ values.

## V Luminosity function

With the use of our systematic and controlled ZTF CLU event sample, we determine a luminosity function for Type IIP and LLIIP SNe. The CLU LLIIP sample nearly triples the current number of published LLIIP SNe in the literature. Our final sample comprises 330 Type IIP SNe, with 36 ( $\approx$ 11%) LLIIP SNe ( $M_{r}>-16$ mag).

We use the $r$ -band photometry to measure the SN II luminosity function and volumetric rate. A volume correction is applied to the luminosity function by weighting each object by $V_{max}=1/D^{3}_{max}$ , where $D_{max}$ ( $\propto 10^{\frac{1}{5}(20-M_{r},peak)}$ ) is the farthest distance at which a transient can be detected given a limiting magnitude of 20 mag. For sources detectable past 150 Mpc, $D_{max}$ was set to the maximum CLU experiment distance of 150 Mpc.

We also correct for the CLU spectroscopic completeness and the ZTF pipeline recovery efficiency factor as they are dependent on the apparent magnitude. Of the total of 2064 transients that are saved in CLU, 1745 (84.6%) transients are classified. The overall completeness of the CLU survey as a function of peak apparent magnitude is indicated by the dashed black line in Figure 4. There are 79 transients for which we are uncertain whether they are real transients on the basis of their spectroscopic and photometric properties. If we exclude these, the overall completeness is $\sim$ 87% (solid black line). Also, we note that the long-lived nature and relative ease of identifying the H $\alpha$ P-Cygni feature make Type IIP events easier to classify. So the Type IIP SNe completeness is likely to be higher than the solid black line. As a conservative estimate, for the rest of the paper, we use the spectroscopic completeness depicted by the dashed black line.

The ZTF image subtraction pipeline has two potential sources of inefficiency relevant to this calculation. In each science image, the pipeline actively masks pixels affected by quality criteria, such as saturation from high brightness, cosmic rays, and defective pixels. This dynamic masking does not have a significant effect as Type IIP SNe have long durations ( $\sim$ 100 days) and are eventually detected by the pipeline. A significant issue relates to the decreased efficiency of the image subtraction algorithm for faint alerts and on bright galaxy backgrounds. Here, we model the efficiency of the ZTF pipeline as a function of the alert flux and the ratio of background surface brightness to target flux. To estimate this, we check whether alert photometry exists for a given epoch for which there is a $\geq 5\sigma$ forced photometry detection. The local host surface brightness is extracted using PS1 $r$ -band images with a 3 $"$ radius aperture. To estimate the conditional probability of the ZTF pipeline efficiency, we consider the binary data, $X$ , which represents whether the ZTF pipeline successfully recovers a transient in alerts ( $X=1$ ) or not ( $X=0$ ). We model $X$ using the Bernoulli distribution:

$$ X\sim\text{Bern}(p), $$

where $p$ is parameterized by a logistic function dependent on the ratio ( $r$ ) of the host surface brightness and the target flux:

$$ p(r)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(a(r-c))}, $$

with $a$ and $c$ representing the model parameters that need to be determined. The logistic function was chosen because it smoothly transitions from 1 to 0 and captures the pipeline efficiency behavior as a function of $r$ . We then estimate the model parameters using the emcee package [34]. The best-fit values of $a$ and $c$ are $a=1.12^{+0.02}_{-0.02}$ and $c=0.21^{+0.03}_{-0.03}$ respectively. As expected, the recovery efficiency decreases as this ratio increases. The best-fit efficiency is $\sim 50\%$ when the host surface brightness and target fluxes are comparable.

We also measure the inefficiency as a function of the apparent magnitude alone, using

$$ p(m)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(b(m-d))}, $$

where $m$ is the alert apparent magnitude. The best-fit values obtained are $b=2.28^{+0.03}_{-0.04}$ mag-1 and $d=20.57^{+0.01}_{-0.01}$ mag. The best fits, and corner plots of the MCMC fit are shown in Figure 5 and Appendix C, respectively. The best-fit efficiency decreases with an increase in target alert apparent magnitude and is $\approx$ 80% when the alert magnitude is 20 mag.

We then weight each SN by the corresponding classification completeness factor and the pipeline efficiency factor. The luminosity function thus obtained is shown in Figure 6 in blue. The luminosity function without volume correction is shown by the green dashed lines in Figure 6. After volume-, incompleteness- and pipeline-efficiency correction, the fraction of LLIIP SNe is $19^{+3}_{-4}\%$ of the entire Type II SN population (see Figure 9). The fraction of Type IIP SNe fainter than $-15$ mag and $-14.5$ are $<5\%$ and $<1.5\%$ respectively.

## VI The Volumetric rate of Type IIP SNe using skysurvey

First, we create a template $r$ -band lightcurve by compiling the photometry data for all the Type IIP SNe in the sample and apply Gaussian Regression processing (Figure 7). We use the skysurvey code44 4 https://github.com/MickaelRigault/skysurvey to estimate the volumetric rate. skysurvey simulates light curves as they would be observed based on a light curve template (using sncosmo) and survey plan. The survey plan is constructed using the actual pointing schedule of ZTF, detailing observation times, the filters used, and the sky brightness. Additionally, the simulation incorporates data on CCD outlines to account for data losses caused by chip gaps.

For the selection of simulated SNe II from skysurvey, we use the forced photometry-based selection criteria outlined in Section II.2. We require at least two 5 $\sigma$ detections exceeding 20 mag in brightness. These criteria guarantee detection by the ZTF alert system, allowing the transient to pass the CLU filter, with a distance $<150$ Mpc to ensure appropriate CLU filter saving and spectroscopic follow-up. Additionally, the lightcurve quality cuts described in Section II.2 are employed to consistently filter the skysurvey sample.

We generate ZTF lightcurves of Type IIP SNe for a range of input volumetric rates ( $0.1$ – $10.0\times 10^{4}\ \textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ ) for the skysurvey simulation up to a distance of 150 Mpc, according to the luminosity function in Figure 6. At each rate, 30 survey plan simulations were conducted. For these simulations, we documented the number of transients that successfully passed the filtering process. The detection estimate for each rate was made by computing the mean number of transients detected from the simulations, with the standard deviation serving as the error estimate. Figure 8 shows the expected number of detected transients along with the fraction of simulations that yield our observed sample size within an error margin of 10% for a given input volumetric rate.

The fraction of simulations matching our sample size follows a skewed Gaussian distribution, which was used to estimate the rate and its uncertainty based on a 68% confidence interval. This analysis yields a volumetric rate of $(2.6_{-0.3}^{+0.3})\times 10^{4}\ \textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ .

This raw skysurvey rate already accounts for survey conditions such as weather and cadence as we used the real observing history of ZTF to simulate the light curves as they would have been observed. We now apply corrections for spectroscopic incompleteness, pipeline recovery efficiency and galaxy catalog incompleteness. As shown in Section V, the CLU experiment achieved an overall completeness rate of $\approx$ 84%.

In the CLU experiment, our methodology restricts the identification of SNe to those in galaxies where a spectroscopic redshift has been established. Therefore, we must correct the skysurvey rate of LLIIP events for galaxy catalog incompleteness. To correct for the incompleteness of the galaxy catalog, we used the redshift completeness factor derived from the ZTF Bright Transient Survey [39]. We use the redshifts and WISE 3.36 $\mu m$ absolute magnitudes (MW1) of the host galaxies of our sample and weight each event by 1/RCF(z,MW1) to estimate the effect of galaxy catalog incompleteness (see Figure 10). This leads to an underestimate of the volumetric rate by $\approx$ 19%.

Finally, as mentioned earlier, the ZTF image subtraction pipeline has a reduced efficiency of the image subtraction algorithm on bright galaxy backgrounds and fainter targets. We weight each event by the inverse of the Pipeline Efficiency Factor (1/PEF(M, host)). This leads to an underestimate of the rate by $\approx$ 6%.

Applying the corrections described above, we derive a corrected rate of $(3.9_{-0.4}^{+0.4})\times 10^{4}\ \textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for Type IIP SNe and $(7.3_{-0.6}^{+0.6})\times 10^{3}\ \textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \textrm{yr}^{-1}$ for LLIIP SNe.
